theme: Hezekiah’s illness and recovery; the Babylonian envoys
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 38:1-39:8. Hezekiah becomes ill, prays, and is given fifteen more years. Then he makes a mistake with the Babylonian envoys. Read the prayer of thanks in 38:9-20, and notice the sober ending.
settingTheScene: This is the last section of the historical interlude. In about 703 BC, Hezekiah became deathly ill. The prophet told him to set his house in order, because he would die. The king turned his face to the wall and prayed. God heard and added fifteen years to his life. Then envoys arrived from Merodach-baladan of Babylon, ostensibly to congratulate him. The story serves as a hinge: the Assyrian threat is over, but the Babylonian one is coming.
observation: “Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover” (38:1).
“Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD” (38:2).
“Remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart” (38:3).
“I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life” (38:5).
“Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back” (38:17).
“For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you” (38:18).
“And Hezekiah was pleased, and showed them his treasure house” (39:2).
“Days are coming, when all that is in your house… shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left” (39:6).
interpretation:
The illness comes at the same time as the Assyrian threat, perhaps in the same year. For Hezekiah, the news that he would die meant more than personal loss. He had no son, and the Davidic line seemed at risk. He weeps bitterly and prays. His prayer is honest: remember how I have walked before you. It is not self-righteous but an appeal to the covenant relationship. And God answers. “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears.” He gives a sign: the shadow on the stairway goes backward ten steps.

Hezekiah’s psalm records his experience. He describes his life cut off like a weaver rolling up a cloth. He moans like a dove. And then comes the turning point in verse 17: “In love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.” It is one of the most beautiful phrases in the Bible about forgiveness. What was behind God’s back is out of his sight. And the king concludes that the living thank God: “The fathers make known to the children your faithfulness.” The purpose of his extra years is to praise and to pass faith on.

Then chapter 39 delivers the sad aftermath. When the envoys of Babylon come, Hezekiah is flattered and shows them everything in his house and in all his realm. It may have been vanity, or a political move to find allies against Assyria. Either way, he looked to a human power instead of to God. Isaiah’s rebuke is solemn: everything will go to Babylon, and some of your own sons will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

Hezekiah’s reply is the most unsettling part: “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good. For there will be peace and security in my days.” He accepts the word but seems concerned only with his own lifetime. The man who cried out for his life does not cry out for his descendants. Even great believers can be weak in the face of success.
connection: Micah 7:19 says God will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea, and Colossians 2:13-14 says Christ canceled the record of debt. Psalm 103:12 says he removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. James 5:14-16 teaches us to pray for the sick. 2 Timothy 4:7 shows Paul finishing the race well, a contrast with Hezekiah’s mixed ending. Jesus warns in Luke 12:15-21 about the rich man who thinks only of his own ease.
application:
Thank God for any season of extra time, health, or opportunity, and ask what he wants you to do with it.

Pray for the generation after you, as Hezekiah’s psalm says: make known God’s faithfulness to the children.

Ask whether you have shown your treasures to the world in pride. Return the glory to God.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for hearing your prayer and seeing your tears.
Thank him for casting your sins behind his back.
Ask him to keep you from pride in the good he gives.
